chapter.name: Prime Time
chapter.blurb: Factors and multiples explored through jump-size and treasure-hunt games; prime and composite numbers via the Sieve of Eratosthenes; co-prime numbers; prime factorisation and its use in testing co-primality and divisibility; quick divisibility tests for 2, 4, 5, 8 and 10; and a closing set of number-property puzzles.

scope_in.item: List the factors of a number by finding which 'jump sizes' land exactly on it, and list its multiples by counting on in that number's steps
Find the common factors shared by two or three numbers, e.g. the common factors of 14 and 36 are 1 and 2
Find the common multiples shared by two numbers using a table or listing, e.g. the common multiples of 3 and 4 include 12, 24 and 36
Solve word problems that require finding common factors or common multiples (the treasure-hunt jump-size and idli-vada style problems)
Definition of a perfect number (the sum of all its factors equals twice the number) and identifying an example, such as 6 or 28
Definition of a prime number as a number with exactly two factors, 1 and itself, and of a composite number as one with more than two factors
The number 1 is neither prime nor composite
Use the Sieve of Eratosthenes to list all primes up to 100
Identify primes and composites in a given range, and reason about true/false statements involving primes (e.g. the only even prime, twin primes, a product of two primes is composite)
Definition: two numbers are co-prime if their only common factor is 1
Check whether a given pair of numbers is co-prime by listing and comparing their factors
Find the prime factorisation of a composite number by repeatedly splitting it into factors until only primes remain
The prime factorisation of a number is unique, apart from the order of its prime factors
Find the prime factorisation of a product of two numbers by combining the factorisations of each number
Use prime factorisation to test whether two numbers are co-prime (no common prime factor)
Use prime factorisation to test whether one number is divisible by another (the second number's factorisation is fully contained in the first's)
Test for divisibility by 10 (last digit is 0), by 5 (last digit is 0 or 5), and by 2 (last digit is 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8)
Test for divisibility by 4 using the last two digits, and by 8 using the last three digits
Apply the divisibility tests for 2, 4, 5, 8 and 10 together to a given number, and find remainders on division by 10, 5 and 2
Apply the divisibility-by-4 test to determine leap years, including the century-year exception (divisible by 100 but not by 400)
Given a small set of numbers, use factors, multiples, primes and composites (from this chapter) to identify which number differs from the rest by a stated property

scope_out.item: HCF (GCD) and LCM by name, and the division-ladder or prime-factorisation shortcut methods for computing them
scope_out.reason: This chapter builds only 'common factors' and 'common multiples' as list-and-compare ideas; HCF/LCM terminology and computation shortcuts are introduced in a later chapter, not here
The chapter explicitly defers these: 'We will discuss simple methods to test divisibility by 3, 6, 7, and 9 in later classes!' (p.125)

scope_out.item: Proof of why the last-two-digit and last-three-digit divisibility tests for 4 and 8 actually work
scope_out.reason: The book poses this as an open 'Math Talk' discussion question, not as content to be tested; only the rule and its application are established

scope_out.item: Euclid's proof that there are infinitely many primes
scope_out.reason: Mentioned only as a forward-looking teaser -- 'A mathematician named Euclid found the answer and so will you in a later class!' (p.114) -- not taught here

scope_out.item: Square numbers / perfect squares as a formal topic
scope_out.reason: The word 'square' appears only as one student's informal aside in the Section 5.6 discussion (p.126); squares are not defined or taught anywhere in this chapter

scope_out.item: The peg-and-thread co-prime art activity and the prime-factor grid puzzle in Section 5.6
scope_out.reason: These are purely visual/spatial enrichment activities with no single written answer, unsuited to a text-based question

scope_out.item: Long division as a method for testing whether a number is a factor of another
scope_out.reason: The chapter's whole point in Sections 5.4-5.5 is to avoid long division, using prime factorisation and last-digit patterns instead

concepts.name: Factors, Multiples, Common Factors and Common Multiples
concepts.description: Listing the factors and multiples of a number, and finding the common factors and common multiples shared by two or more numbers.
concepts.idea: A factor of a number divides it exactly, like a jump size that lands on it; a multiple is what you get by scaling a number up. Numbers that are factors of two numbers at once, or multiples of two numbers at once, are their common factors or common multiples.
concepts.rule: The factors of a number are the whole numbers that divide it with zero remainder; its multiples are obtained by multiplying it by 1, 2, 3, and so on. A common factor of two numbers divides both of them, and a common multiple of two numbers is a multiple of both.
concepts.example: The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. The factors of 18 are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. Their common factors are 1, 2, 3 and 6.

concepts.name: Prime and Composite Numbers
concepts.description: Identifying prime numbers (exactly two factors) and composite numbers (more than two factors), and using the Sieve of Eratosthenes to list primes.
concepts.idea: Arranging a number of objects into a rectangle shows its factors; a number that can only be arranged in a single row has just two factors and is prime.
concepts.rule: A number with exactly two factors, 1 and itself, is prime. A number with more than two factors is composite. The number 1 has only one factor, so it is neither prime nor composite.
concepts.example: 7 has only the factors 1 and 7, so it is prime. 12 has factors 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12, so it is composite.

concepts.name: Co-prime Numbers
concepts.description: Determining whether two numbers are co-prime, that is, whether their only common factor is 1.
concepts.idea: In the treasure-jump game, if a jump size of 1 is the only one that reaches both treasure numbers, the numbers are 'safe' -- they share no bigger common factor.
concepts.rule: Two numbers are co-prime if the only common factor between them is 1. If they share any common factor bigger than 1, they are not co-prime.
concepts.example: The factors of 4 are 1, 2, 4 and the factors of 9 are 1, 3, 9; their only common factor is 1, so 4 and 9 are co-prime.

concepts.name: Prime Factorisation and Its Uses
concepts.description: Writing a number as a product of primes, and using that prime factorisation to test whether two numbers are co-prime or whether one number divides another.
concepts.idea: Breaking a composite number apart again and again, always splitting any composite piece further, eventually leaves only primes -- and however you split it, the same primes turn up in the end.
concepts.rule: Every number greater than 1 has a prime factorisation that is unique apart from the order of the factors. Two numbers are co-prime exactly when they share no common prime factor; one number is divisible by another exactly when the second number's prime factorisation is fully contained within the first's.
concepts.example: 72 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 x 3. Since 12 = 2 x 2 x 3 is contained within this (two 2s and one 3), 72 is divisible by 12.

questions.q: A classmate concludes that since 80 and 63 have no common prime factor, they must have no common factor of any kind other than 1. Judge this reasoning.

Since 80 = 2x2x2x2x5 and 63 = 3x3x7 share no prime, they cannot share any factor greater than 1 either.
s: Judges the reasoning to be correct
Explains why using the link between composite common factors and prime factors

concepts.name: Divisibility Tests for 2, 4, 5, 8 and 10
concepts.description: Testing whether a number is divisible by 2, 4, 5, 8 or 10 by inspecting only its last digit or last few digits, without long division.
concepts.idea: Because 10 is divisible by 2 and by 5, only the very last digit of a number decides its divisibility by 2, 5 and 10; testing 4 and 8 needs a couple more digits since 10 itself is not divisible by 4 or 8.
concepts.rule: Divisible by 10 if it ends in 0. Divisible by 5 if it ends in 0 or 5. Divisible by 2 if it ends in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. Divisible by 4 if the number formed by its last two digits is divisible by 4. Divisible by 8 if the number formed by its last three digits is divisible by 8.
concepts.example: 8536 ends in 36, and 36 is divisible by 4, so 8536 is divisible by 4.

questions.q: Explain why checking the last digit is enough to test divisibility by 2, but is not enough to test divisibility by 4.
questions.a: For divisibility by 2, only the last digit decides the remainder when dividing by 2, since 10 itself is divisible by 2. But 10 is not divisible by 4, so looking at just the last digit is not enough -- numbers like 12 and 22 share the last digit 2, yet 12 is divisible by 4 and 22 is not.
s: Explains why the last digit alone works for divisibility by 2
Gives the 12-vs-22 (or similar) example showing the last digit alone fails for 4

questions.q: Which pair of numbers shows that divisibility by 4 cannot be decided by the last digit alone?
questions.a: 12 and 22

questions.q: Which of the following is divisible by 8?
8536 is divisible by 4 because its last two digits, 36, are divisible by ____.
Which of the following numbers is divisible by both 2 and 5?
The teacher asked if 14560 is divisible by 2, 4, 5, 8 and 10. Guna checked only two of these and declared it divisible by all five. Which two could he have checked, and why is that enough?
questions.a: Checking divisibility by 8 and by 5 is enough. If the last three digits (560) are divisible by 8, the number is automatically divisible by 2 and 4 as well. If it also ends in 0 (divisible by 5), it is automatically divisible by 10 too, since ending in 0 covers both the 2-test and the 5-test.
s: Identifies checking 8 and 5 (or an equivalent valid pair) as sufficient
Explains why passing the harder test (8) guarantees the easier ones, and why ending in 0 covers both 5 and 10

questions.q: Find the remainder when 173 is divided by (a) 10, (b) 5, (c) 2.
questions.a: (a) Divided by 10, the remainder is 3, since 173 ends in 3. (b) Divided by 5, the remainder is 3, since the nearest lower multiple of 5 is 170. (c) Divided by 2, the remainder is 1, since 173 is odd.
s: Gives the correct remainder 3 on division by 10 and by 5
Gives the correct remainder 1 on division by 2

Find the largest 4-digit number that is divisible by 4 and is also a palindrome (reads the same forwards and backwards).
questions.a: A 4-digit palindrome has the form ABBA. Testing the largest candidates downward using the last-two-digit rule for 4: 9999 (ends 99, not divisible by 4), 9889 (ends 89, no), ..., 8998 (ends 98, no), 8888 (ends 88, and 88 divided by 4 = 22, divisible). No palindrome between 8888 and 9999 works, so the largest 4-digit palindrome divisible by 4 is 8888.
s: Recognises the ABBA palindrome structure for 4-digit numbers
Tests candidates from the largest downward using the last-two-digit rule for 4
Identifies 8888 as the largest 4-digit palindrome divisible by 4

questions.q: Consider: (I) If the last two digits of a number are divisible by 4, the whole number is divisible by 4. (II) If a number is divisible by 4, its last two digits must be divisible by 4. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Both I and II

questions.q: A student claims: 'Any number ending in 6 is divisible by both 2 and 4.' Test this on 16, 26 and 36, and state whether the claim is fully correct.
questions.a: All of 16, 26, 36 end in 6, so all are divisible by 2. Checking divisibility by 4: 16 divided by 4 = 4 (divisible), 26 divided by 4 = 6.5 (not divisible), 36 divided by 4 = 9 (divisible). So the '4' part of the claim is false -- ending in 6 guarantees divisibility by 2 but not by 4, as 26 shows.
s: Confirms all three numbers are divisible by 2 since they end in an even digit

questions.q: A classmate says, 'Testing divisibility by 8 needs only the last digit, just like testing divisibility by 2.' Judge this statement.
questions.a: The statement is false. Divisibility by 2 depends only on the last digit because 10 itself is divisible by 2. But 10 is not divisible by 8, so divisibility by 8 depends on the last three digits, not just the last one.
s: Judges the statement to be false
Explains the difference in reasoning between the tests for 2 and for 8, referencing the last-three-digit rule

questions.q: Construct a 4-digit number that is divisible by both 4 and 10, but NOT by 8. Show it satisfies all three conditions.
questions.a: Take 1420. Divisible by 10: yes, it ends in 0. Divisible by 4: its last two digits are 20, and 20 divided by 4 = 5, so yes. Divisible by 8? Its last three digits are 420, and 420 divided by 8 = 52.5, not a whole number, so 1420 is NOT divisible by 8. All three conditions are satisfied.
s: Selects a 4-digit number ending in 0
Verifies divisibility by 4 and by 10 correctly
Verifies the number is not divisible by 8, using the last three digits

concepts.name: Special Numbers: Reasoning with Factors, Multiples, Primes and Composites
concepts.description: Given a small set of numbers, using the chapter's ideas -- factors, multiples, primes and composites -- to identify which number is set apart from the rest by a stated property.
concepts.idea: The same set of numbers can be described in more than one way; noticing what makes one number different uses exactly the vocabulary this chapter has built up.
concepts.rule: To find what makes a number special in a set, test each number against a stated property -- prime or composite, a multiple of some number, or divisible by some number -- and see which one differs from the rest.
concepts.example: In the set 9, 16, 25, 43: 9, 16 and 25 are all composite (3x3, 4x4, 5x5), while 43 is prime, so 43 is the odd one out.

s: Identifies 41 as the only prime

questions.q: In the set 12, 20, 27, 28, three numbers are multiples of 4 and one is not. Identify the exception and verify using the last-two-digit test for divisibility by 4.
questions.a: 27 is the exception. Its last two digits are 27, and 27 divided by 4 = 6.75, not a whole number, so 27 is not a multiple of 4. Checking the others: 12 divided by 4 = 3, 20 divided by 4 = 5, 28 divided by 4 = 7, all whole numbers.
s: Identifies 27 as the exception

questions.a: 44 = 2 x 2 x 11 (no 7). 63 = 3 x 3 x 7 (has 7). 77 = 7 x 11 (has 7). 91 = 7 x 13 (has 7). So 44 is the only number without 7 as a prime factor.
s: Finds the prime factorisation of all four numbers correctly

Identifies 44 as the only one without 7 as a factor

questions.q: A student looks at the set 9, 16, 25, 43 and says, '43 is special because it is the only two-digit number that starts with 4.' Evaluate whether this is a mathematically meaningful reason, compared to the reason that 43 is the only prime number in the set.
questions.a: The student's reason (starting with the digit 4) is not a genuine mathematical property -- it depends only on how the number is written, not on any factor, multiple or prime/composite relationship. The better reason is that 9, 16 and 25 are all composite (9=3x3, 16=4x4, 25=5x5) while 43 is prime, since being prime or composite does not depend on how the numeral happens to be written.
s: Explains why the digit-based reason is not a genuine mathematical property
States the composite-vs-prime distinction correctly with factorisations
Concludes the prime/composite reason is the mathematically meaningful one

questions.q: A classmate says, 'In any set of four numbers, there is always exactly one number that is prime.' Judge this claim using the set 4, 6, 8, 10 as a test case.
questions.a: The claim is false. In the set 4, 6, 8, 10, none of the numbers is prime -- all four are even numbers greater than 2, so each has 2 as an extra factor and is composite. A set of four numbers need not contain exactly one prime; it can contain none at all.
s: Judges the claim to be false
Supports this using the set 4, 6, 8, 10, showing all four are composite

questions.q: Construct a set of four numbers, each between 10 and 30, such that exactly one number is prime and the other three are composite. Show the prime/composite check for all four.
questions.a: Take 14, 21, 23, 27. Checking each: 14 = 2 x 7, composite. 21 = 3 x 7, composite. 23 has only the factors 1 and 23, so it is prime. 27 = 3 x 3 x 3, composite. So exactly one number, 23, is prime, and the other three are composite, as required.
s: Chooses four numbers between 10 and 30
Checks each number for primality/compositeness correctly
Confirms exactly one prime and three composite numbers in the final set
